entry.title: Quantumania 18 - Mixed Messages
entry.content:
We’ve considered measurable things, such as which way something is pointing in space, and the framework we’ve given for that implied that the only kinds of physical measurement we can do involve measuring in one basis. That is, all the possible outcomes of the measurement correspond to orthogonal state vectors, giving us a very convenient basis in which to capture the state vector in coordinates, such that each coordinate gives us one of the outcomes.

Another way to write this is as follows. If $\ket{M_n}$ is the vector associated with the $n$-th measurement outcome, and clearly our state vector $\ket{\psi}$ can be thought of as a column vector written in the basis $\lbrace \ket{M_1}, \ket{M_2} \dots \rbrace$, then:

\[\braket{M_n}{\psi}\]

in effect means “pluck the $n$-th coordinate out of $\psi$”.

Recalling that if you switch the labels on a bra-ket it’s the complex conjugate, and to convert the $n$-th coordinate into the probability of obtaining the $n$-th measurement outcome we need to multiply it by its own complex conjugate, that probability can be written:

\[\braket{\psi}{M_n} \braket{M_n}{\psi}\]

But we’ve written it in a way that doesn’t assume anything about a coordinate representation in any basis. We’re using operations with a geometrical meaning: the inner product of two vectors, which is invariant, completely independent of the choice of basis. We know our state vector could be described in the measurement basis, that is, there must be some column of complex coordinates $c_n$ such that:

\[\ket{\psi} = \sum_n \ket{M_n} c_n\]

And we can use the inner product to get those coordinates, $c_n = \braket{M_n}{\psi}$. Substituting:

\[\ket{\psi} = \sum_n \ket{M_n} \braket{M_n}{\psi}\]

In that expression our eye is naturally drawn to the familiar bra-ket pattern, which we should be in the habit of seeing as a scalar. So the expression inside the sum builds a vector that is colinear with $\ket{M_n}$, as that’s what we’re scaling. But let’s pull out this part by itself:

\[\ket{M_n} \bra{M_n}\]

We could call this a ket-bra, I guess? Nobody does though. Given that the bra-ket’s official name is the inner product, it’s easy to remember the ket-bra’s official name, the outer product. The role played by this object in our example is to operate on a vector to product another vector, and so it’s an operator and can be represented by a matrix. In fact, if we have a column vector representing $\ket{M_n}$, and we use the hermitian conjugate to get a row vector representing $\bra{M_n}$, writing them side-by-side in ket bra order is simply matrix multiplication:

\[P_n = \ket{M_n} \bra{M_n} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a^* & b^* \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a a^* & a b^* \\ b a^* & b b^* \end{bmatrix}\]

So for the basis vectors in the measurement basis:

\[P_1 = \ket{M_1} \bra{M_1} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad P_2 = \ket{M_2} \bra{M_2} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

These are called projection operators, because when applied to a vector $\ket{\psi}$, they project it onto the vector they were built from. $P_1$ flattens a vector into alignment with $\ket{M_1}$, making the component vector of $\ket{\psi}$ along $\ket{M_1}$, or $c_1 \ket{M_1}$ where $c_1$ is the first coordinate of $\ket{\psi}$ in the $M$ basis. So if used like this:

\[\bra{\psi} P_n \ket{\psi} = \braket{\psi}{M_n} \braket{M_n}{\psi} = c_n^* c_n\]

So we go straight to the probability of obtaining the $n$-th measurement outcome from state $\bra{\psi}$. Why bother to think of the middle operator as new type of thing? Because this allows us to generalise the idea of a measurable outcome to include non-orthogonal possibilities. Measuring equipment isn’t always as ideal as we might imagine.

Even so, we can see how this looser way of defining measurement can be applied if we imagine a scenario that is still idealised, but in a different way to usual. Suppose Alice is going to receive (from Bob, of course) a qubit and all she knows is that its state is going to be either $\ket{0}$ or $\ket{+}$. That is, either a basis state of the Z basis, or a basis state of the X basis. Welcoming back our old friend (don’t worry, there’s a whole new diagram coming up):

These two possibilities are not orthogonal. They’re at $45^\circ$ to one another. Each is a basis vector of one basis that can be expressed as a balanced superposition of the other basis.

If Alice measures in the Z basis she might find $\ket{1}$. As she knows Bob definitely didn’t send her that, she can conclude he definitely sent $\ket{+}$ and it just flipped randomly into the $\ket{1}$ state. If he’d sent the other option, $\ket{0}$, she would have measured that with certainty, because it’s a basis vector of the basis she’s measuring in.

But if she finds $\ket{0}$, what does that tell her? Bob could have sent her $\ket{0}$, but equally he could have sent $\ket{+}$ and it flipped into $\ket{0}$, as it randomly might. She could reason in much the same way about a measurement on the X basis. Whichever basis she chooses to measure in, the outcome is certain for one of the possibilities, occurring half the time (assuming Bob makes an unbiased random choice of what to send), and “Who knows?” for the other half.

The only way to improve on this is to make a trade-off: to accept getting a “Who knows?” answer more than half the time, but in exchange sometimes getting an absolutely certain answer for whichever qubit Bob sends. Mathematically the core of this is the orthogonal complement.

To picture this, think of a plane surface, orientated at some interesting angle. Then think of light rays shining on it so they are perfectly perpendicular to the plane. Now imagine a stick attached to the plane and sticking out from it. If the stick is itself perpendicular to the plane it won’t cast a shadow, because it’s in line with the light rays. But if the stick is tilted away from the perpendicular, it will cast a shadow. The shadow is the stick’s component in the plane.

We can think of this as a 3D vector space if we visualise the origin as the point where the stick is attached to the plane. How can a plane exist in a vector space? Easy: it’s a set of vectors. The plane is a 2D subspace of the 3D space, containing all the vectors that lie in the plane.

We can turn the stick into the shadow by applying a projection operator that flattens 3D vectors into that 2D subspace. To construct that operator, suppose we know the vector $\ket{v}$ that is normal (orthogonal) to the plane, that is, it’s orthogonal to any vector lying in the plane. This is the vector that wouldn’t cast any shadow. Then we work out this operator:

\[I - \ket{v} \bra{v}\]

It’s the projection operator on to $\ket{v}$ subtracted from the identity operator. So if we represent all this in coordinates such that $\ket{v}$ is the first basis vector:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}\]

The resulting matrix very clearly discards the first coordinate (the $\ket{v}$ direction) but retains the information from the other two (the plane), so flattens whatever vector it applies to into its shadow on the plane. And if applied a second time to that shadow, it will have no effect. The shadow exists in the 2D plane that is represented by the $2 \times 2$ square matrix in the lower right, which looks uncannily like the 2D identity matrix, because it is. To qualify as a projection operator, we only require that an operator is:

  • hermitian (self-adjoint): $P^\dagger = P$
  • idempotent: $P^2 = P$ (if applied a second time, it makes no difference, the damage is done.)

Now, in our example with qubits the space is two dimensional, so projection operators can only project onto lines, not planes.

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}\]

So in 2D, the orthogonal complement of a vector is not a plane, it’s just another vector, although it is orthogonal to the original. But I wanted to get across the general idea as it pertains to higher dimensional vector spaces because that’s what we’re dealing with when we have more than one qubit.

Also, bear in mind that the kind of measurement we’re going to talk about next makes use of orthogonal complements to projection operators, which are themselves projection operators, and yet the official term “projective measurement” is reserved for the kind of measurement we’ve previously talked about, where we choose a basis to measure in, and the probabilities of obtaining the outcomes are found by projecting the state vector onto the basis vectors.

Back to Alice and Bob. Alice wants three measurement outcomes: two are definite answers: $\ket{0}$ or $\ket{+}$, and the other is “don’t know.” It’s okay if she gets a lot of don’t-knows, as long as she never gets a confidently wrong answer.

By sending the qubit through certain purely unitary transformations, it is possible to effectively send it into the path of three detectors, each of which does an ordinary projective measurement (that is, measuring in a specific basis just as we’ve always talked about), but only one of the three detectors will actually detect something, because although we can’t say anything for sure about how the qubit travels to its destination, it ultimately “collapses” to one of the three possible destinations. Alice makes it so that one of the detectors has zero probability of detecting something if the input qubit was $\ket{0}$, another has zero probability for $\ket{+}$, and the third mops up the remaining probability.

More precisely, the first detector’s probability of firing for a qubit in state $\ket{\psi}$ is:

\[\bra{\psi} E_1 \ket{\psi}\]

where

\[E_1 \propto I - \ket{0} \bra{0}\]

(Note that it’s proportional-to, rather than equal-to: there would be an overall scaling factor to make sure the probabilities add to $1$.)

The projection $E_1$ obliterates any component in the $\ket{0}$ direction. If the qubit is exactly $\ket{0}$, it has a zero-length shadow in this projection. There’s a similar $E_2$ that obliterates $\ket{+}$. Finally, the don’t-know detector is just:

\[E_? = I - (E_1 + E_2)\]

It’s the complement of the sum of the other two complements: it throws away that which would cause the either of the other two to cast a shadow.

So Bob sends $\ket{0}$, detector 2 is the only one that definitely won’t fire. If he sends $\ket{+}$, detector 1 cannot fire. Either way, detector 3 always has a probability of firing, so Alice will get a lot of don’t-knows. But if detector 1 fires, she knows for absolute certain that Bob sent $\ket{0}$, and if 2 fires she knows he sent $\ket{+}$.

entry.title: Quantumania 17 - More Function, More Mystery
entry.content:
We ended up being slightly less impressed than we might have been about the Hadamard gate’s ability to narrow down the identity of a mystery function from four possibilities to two with a single measurement, given that we could make the same amount of progress by invoking the function once directly. If you give the function $0$ as the input, it can only output $0$ or $1$, and that divides the four possible functions into two pairs.

Even so, there’s still something neat about the idea that we’ve “rotated a function” so that we can, with a single invocation, narrow it down to being either a constant that ignores its input or being dependent on its input, something that seems to absolutely require two invocations. I used the term balanced for the latter kind, in anticipation of the upgrade we’re going to embark on today.

That upgrade is going to show off our ability to casually string together many qubits into a register of qubits. I think it’s quite cool that we’re using terminology from classical computing. Registers in this context, as in mechanisms for temporarily storing numbers, have existed for as long as mechanical calculators (hundreds of years.) A long time ago there was something called a cash register (ask your grandma.)

We can build states for compound systems of three qubits by using the tensor product to stitch their spaces together:

\[\ket{0} \otimes \ket{0} \otimes \ket{0} = \ket{000}\]

Rather than writing out absurdly long kets as we increase the number of qubits to a large number $n$, you’ll sometimes see this notation:

\[\ket{0} ^{\otimes n}\]

We’re just raising $\ket{0}$ to the power of $n$ (but using the tensor product.) So that’s a really quick way to say I have a system of $n$ qubits. Now, with such a system I can apply a unitary operation like Hadamard (symbolised here by $H$) to individual qubits:

\[H \ket{0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{0} + \ket{1} \Big)\]

If I have two qubits in $\ket{0}$ and put each through Hadamard, and multiply out:

\[H \ket{0} \otimes H \ket{0} = \frac{1}{2} \Big( \ket{0} + \ket{1} \Big) \Big( \ket{0} + \ket{1} \Big) = \frac{1}{2} \Big( \ket{00} + \ket{01} + \ket{10} + \ket{11} \Big)\]

Now for the first time (it’s a big day) we’re actually going to interpret the bit patterns in qubit tensor products as actual binary numbers. What happens if we have a system of $8$ qubits, in which $\ket{00101010}$ would signify $42$, but ours are initially all zero, and put each them through Hadamard and multiply out?

\[\frac{1}{16} \Big( \ket{00000000} + \ket{00000001} + \ket{00000010} + \cdots \ket{11111101} + \ket{11111110} + \ket{11111111} \Big)\]

It’s an equal superposition of every number in the range $0$ to $255$. Why is the normalisation factor $1/16$? Because this is Pythagoras in $256$ dimensions: all those ingredients are unit vectors, the square of the length of each is $1$, there are $256$ of them, so the square of the “hypotenuse” of this ultra-hyper-bonkers-triangle is $256$, thus its length is $\sqrt{256} = 16$, so that’s what we need to divide by to shrink it down to $1$.

In general, for $n$ qubits treated in this way the result is the state vector:

\[\ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}} \sum_{x = 0}^{2^n - 1} \ket{x}\]

Here $x$ can be thought of the value between $0$ and $2^n - 1$ but represented in binary and used as the label for one of the ingredients.

Now we have what we need to upgrade our mystery function scenario so that function takes an $n$-bit number as its input and produces a single bit as output. But to make this work we’re going to have to introduce a restriction on the mystery function that will seem a little contrived: it either ignores the input number entirely (it’s a constant), or it is balanced, meaning that for exactly half the range of possible values it produces output $1$ and for the other half $0$. Supposing it is balanced, we have no idea which input values produce $1$. To be sure it’s not constant, you’d have to test the function on just over half the possible input values, $2^n/2 + 1$, potentially a huge number.

When we had one-bit input, the mystery function was wrapped in a unitary operator, by passing the first qubit straight through unchanged (at least, according to the definition) and using the result of the function to affect the second qubit’s output.

\[U_f \ket{A, B} = \ket{A, B \oplus f(A)}\]

Now we’re going to do the same thing except $A$ is our qubit register, carrying some $n$-bit number. $B$ is just an extra qubit that will carry the encoded output, and at input it is $H \ket{1} = \ket{-}$, so the complete input state is:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}} \sum_{x = 0}^{2^n - 1} \ket{x} \otimes \ket{-}\]

When $U_f$ acts on this, being linear, it distributes over all the summed terms. Each term is in effect acted on like this:

\[U_f \Big( \ket{x} \otimes \ket{-} \Big) = U_f \left( \ket{x} \otimes \frac{\ket{0} - \ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{0 \oplus f(x)} - \ket{x} \ket{1 \oplus f(x)} \Big)\]

This means that if $f(x) = 0$, it adds nothing and this particular term is unchanged:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{0 \oplus f(x)} - \ket{x} \ket{1 \oplus f(x)} \Big) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{0} - \ket{x} \ket{1} \Big) = \ket{x} \otimes \ket{-}\]

Whereas if $f(x) = 1$ it in effect swaps the labels of the output bit ingredients:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{0 \oplus f(x)} - \ket{x} \ket{1 \oplus f(x)} \Big) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{1} - \ket{x} \ket{0} \Big) = -\ket{x} \otimes \ket{-}\]

A nifty way to capture this optional negative factor effect, given that $(-1)^0 = 1$ and $(-1)^{1} = -1$, is:

\[(-1)^{f(x)}\]

And (like we saw with the single qubit version of this problem), our interest in the extra $\ket{-}$ qubit ends at this point because it is unaffected. We can focus on the input $n$-qubit register, which now looks like this:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}} \sum_{x = 0}^{2^n - 1} (-1)^{f(x)} \ket{x}\]

It’s starting to look a bit garbled, but it’s just saying that the state is the sum of $2^n$ different vector terms that have been flipped to negative if $f(x) = 1$ for term $x$. For example, if $n = 3$ then there are $8$ terms represented by $\ket{x}$ in the sum, such as $\ket{000}$, $\ket{001}$, $\ket{010}$, and so on up to $\ket{111}$. If $f(101) = 1$, then the $\ket{101}$ term will be negative in the sum. And then all will be scaled down by $1/\sqrt{8}$ to make it unitary.

As if it weren’t garbled enough, the last step is (as before) to apply Hadamard one more time. As we saw above, when we apply it to an all-zeros state $\ket{000\dots}$, the result is an expansion containing a term for every bit pattern. Well, now we’re applying it to the sum of terms for every bit pattern. If you’re into coding, this is what you might call a nested loop. Again, supposing $n = 3$, we have a sum of $8$ terms, some positive, some negative, and each of those will now expand out into $8$ terms, some positive, some negative, so we’ll have $64$ terms. But these can then be grouped together because there will be $8$ repetitions of $\ket{000}$, also $8$ of $\ket{001}$, and so on.

Actually multiplying them all out even for $n = 3$ would be rather tedious. It’s more instructive to think through how each term ends up with its effective final sign. The way Hadamard works on the basis vectors is that it only introduces a negative factor when the input is $\ket{1}$, and it only places that negative factor on the output $\ket{1}$ term. So an all-zeros $\ket{000\dots}$ state put through Hadamard produces only positive terms.

With the other terms, those with at least one $1$, something remarkable happens: when we group the remaining $56$ multiplied-out terms into their $7$ types, among the $8$ copies of (say) $\ket{010}$, $4$ are positive and $4$ are negative, so they cancel out. This happens for every basis vector apart from all-zeros. This shouldn’t be that surprising though, as we know that Hadamard is self-inverting: $H = H^{-1}$. So that can only mean:

\[H^2 \ket{000\dots} = \ket{000\dots}\]

So if the mystery function is constant, and thus applies the same sign-flip to every term, there are only two possibilities. If $f(x) = 0$, there’s no overall sign-flip:

\[H U_f H \ket{000\dots} = \ket{000\dots}\]

Whereas if $f(x) = 1$, the sign is flipped:

\[H U_f H \ket{000\dots} = -\ket{000\dots}\]

Either way, this state will with certainty produce a $\ket{0}$ on every qubit. No other pattern has a non-zero amplitude.

The only other form the mystery function is allowed to take is to be balanced, and I said that was going to seem contrived. What it means for the $\ket{000\dots}$ state is that exactly half the terms contributing to it will be positive and half will be negative, and this will be entirely the function’s doing (Hadamard leaves all-zeros states alone.) The first (inner) Hadamard makes a term for every possible value, all of them positive, the mystery function flips the sign of half of them, and the final (outer) Hadamard creates from each a $\ket{000\dots}$ contribution that preserves the sign of the term it came from. This means that all the $\ket{000\dots}$ contributions cancel out, leaving a zero probability of measuring the all-zeros pattern.

The end result is that a measurement of $\ket{000\dots}$ will only happen if it was absolutely certain to happen, because the mystery function is constant. If it is balanced, $\ket{000\dots}$ is impossible, so something else will be found (at least one qubit will be in the $\ket{1\dots}$ state.)

Because of the peculiar contrivance of the setup, this is not at all useful. But it demonstrates how a quantum algorithm can produce a deterministic result, and seemingly explore a potentially huge problem space in a simple and practically instantaneous process. With $n = 275$ qubits, the number of basis vectors is $2^{275} \approx 10^{82}$, about the number of atoms in the visible universe, and yet we seem to be able to probe the behaviour of a function on all of them, all at once.

entry.title: Quantumania 16 - Diagonal = Easy
entry.content:
A digression before we get back to quantum computing. In our previous linear algebra tomfoolery, something important has been bubbling away, which is the importance of diagonal matrix representation, and what they mean for simplicity. They mean that we can think of the dimensions of the space as being like completely separate, isolated channels, which don’t suffer from any “crosstalk”. It’s like you’re doing several completely independent calculations, with no interference between them.

If you apply $\hat{M} \equiv \operatorname{diag}(M_1, M_2)$ to a vector $\vec{v}$:

\[\hat{M} \vec{v} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} M_1 & 0 \\ 0 & M_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} M_1 v_1 \\ M_2 v_2 \end{bmatrix}\]

it’s like two completely separate conversations on different phone lines. The $n$th diagonal entry is only applicable to the $n$th coordinate of the vector. If any off-diagonal entry was non-zero it would be a different matter. But diagonal matrices are delightfully straightforward.

We can apply the operator $\hat{M}$ twice, and write that as $\hat{M}^2$:

\[\hat{M}^2 \vec{v} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} M_1 & 0 \\ 0 & M_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} M_1 & 0 \\ 0 & M_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} M_1^2 v_1 \\ M_2^2 v_2 \end{bmatrix}\]

In a way this is a function applied to the matrix, but the way that works is trivial: we just apply that function to the separate diagonal entries. We can extend this idea to any function $f$ (an ordinary mapping between numbers). Such a function can be applied to the matrix as a whole, but it’s really just that we are applying the function separately to the individual diagonal entries.

For matrices in general this wouldn’t make sense: a number-valued function of numbers doesn’t know what to do with a matrix. But with a diagonal matrix, we know the non-zero entries act like independent numbers, so we’re essentially “broadcasting” the function wrapping down to the individual entries:

\[f(M) \equiv \begin{bmatrix} f(M_1) & 0 \\ 0 & f(M_2) \end{bmatrix}\]

This leads to the idea of raising something to the power of an operator. It sounds like gibberish until you realise that as long as the operator can be represented by a diagonal matrix, there’s nothing to it.

What kinds of operator can be represented by a diagonal matrix? The answer to this question depends on what kind of basis we allow. If an operator has eigenvectors that are linearly independent and it has as many as there are dimensions in the space, then we can use the eigenvectors as a basis and represent the operator diagonally.

But for two vectors to be linearly independent just means that they aren’t colinear. We want to be more choosy and require that our basis vectors are orthogonal, because our state vector spaces have an inner product with a simple definition that, in order to produce consistent values regardless of the basis, requires that the basis vectors are orthogonal. So in QM we insist on that, and when we speak of changing the basis, we never mean realigning just some of the basis vectors: they all have to rotate properly together, to stay rigidly orthogonal with each other.

With that restriction, in a real vector space the only kind of operator that can be diagonalised is the kind that scales along orthogonal alignments, and it will be represented in any other allowed basis by a symmetrical matrix.

But in complex vector spaces, it’s a lot more interesting than that. A broader set of operators can be diagonalised in an orthogonal basis. Those that can are called normal operators. Also the test for a normal operator is that it commutes with its adjoint. What do we mean by that?

First, adjoint can be thought of as the abstract geometrical equivalent of the conjugate transpose we’ve been using on matrices. So I could have said, much more verbosely, “If you have an operator, $\hat{A}$, and you represent it by a matrix $A$ in some orthogonal basis, and you take the conjugate transpose of that matrix, and those two matrices commute, then $\hat{A}$ is normal.” Also wherever we talked about hermitian matrices, we could instead have talked about self-adjoint operators.

And second, commuting means that two operators can be applied in either order and the result is the same. Again, dropping down to the matrix representation, if you multiply out the two matrices in both orders, the resulting matrix must be the same either way in order for it to be a normal matrix representing a normal operator:

\[A A^\dagger = A^\dagger A \quad \text{for a normal matrix, A}\]

The surprising thing is that as well as self-adjoint operators being normal, so are unitary operators. Rotations can not generally be diagonalised in a real vector space, but in a complex one they can. How, though? Algebraically it follows automatically from the fact that a unitary operator is defined by the requirement that:

\[U U^\dagger = I\]

That is, the inverse of $U$ is its own adjoint. The same must be true going the other way, and so either way around, the result is $I$. It commutes with its own adjoint, so unitary implies normal.

Working more intuitively, in a real vector space we know a diagonal matrix scales along orthogonal directions, with the scaling factors given by the diagonal entries themselves. But a unitary operator isn’t allowed to scale along any direction. It preserves the lengths of all vectors as well as the angles between them. So if it has eigenvectors at all, surely their eigenvalues would have to be $\pm 1$. (In fact in the confines of a 2D real vector space, rotations have no eigenvectors, except rotations by a multiple of $\pi$.)

In a complex space, we find the length of a vector $\ket{v}$ by using the complex form of the inner product, $\braket{v}{v}$ and then taking the square root. This always gives a real number regardless of whether the vector has complex coordinates. So the eigenvalues of our unitary operator could be complex numbers, as long as they have unit modulus, of the form $e^{i\theta}$, lying on the unit circle in the complex plane. The diagonal form of a rotation is like this:

\[\begin{bmatrix} e^{i\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta} \end{bmatrix}\]

The two coordinates rotate in the complex plane in opposite directions. Why is that? The familiar template for a rotation matrix in a real vector space is:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta \end{bmatrix}\]

We can imagine the real space $\mathbb{R}^2$ as being embedded within the complex space $\mathbb{C}^2$. That is, the standard basis vectors (the Z basis, to use their qubit names):

\[\ket{0} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad \ket{1} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

are a pair of ingredients that we can scale and sum using only real coordinates, to build any vector that lies within a “real subspace”. To be precise about what we mean by this, to access the whole space with real coordinates, we’d need a couple more weird ingredients:

\[\ket{\gamma} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} i \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad \ket{\kappa} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ i \end{bmatrix}\]

This would allow us to build the full range of complex vectors from four real coordinates $(a, b, c, d)$:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \ket{\psi} &=& a \ket{0} + b \ket{1} + c \ket{\gamma} + d \ket{\kappa} \\ \\ &\equiv& \begin{bmatrix} a \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ b \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} ci \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ di \end{bmatrix} \\ \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} a + ci \\ b + di \end{bmatrix} \end{eqnarray*}\]

So we’re still building 2D complex vectors in $\mathbb{C}^2$, but we’re approaching it as a 4D real space $\mathbb{R}^4$, and we can restrict ourselves to a 2D real subspace of that if we like.

If we take a pair of these ingredients that aren’t complex multiples of each other, such as $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$, or $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{\kappa}$, and combine them with complex scalars, we can make any complex vector. So such pairs form a basis for the whole $\mathbb{C}^2$ space, and if we pick an orthogonal, unit-norm pair it’s an orthonormal basis. We can also make other orthonormal bases by linear combination of our ingredients. For example:

\[\ket{v_+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big[ \ket{0} - \ket{\kappa} \Big] \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -i \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad \ket{v_-} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big[ \ket{0} + \ket{\kappa} \Big] \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{bmatrix}\]

Why have they been labelled with $+$ and $-$ in apparent opposition to the sign used in their definitions? Because we’re going to be scaling them by complex phase factors that twist them in the positive (anticlockwise) and negative (clockwise) directions respectively, using the diagonalised rotation matrix defined above.

These two vectors are an orthogonal unit basis, as we can test them with the inner product:

\[\braket{v_+}{v_+} = \braket{v_-}{v_-} = 1\] \[\braket{v_+}{v_-} = 0\]

And we can write down the matrix that would convert a vector expressed in this basis into the standard $\ket{0}, \ket{1}$ basis: we just use the definitions of $\ket{v_+}$ and $\ket{v_-}$ as the columns of the matrix:

\[P = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -i & i \end{bmatrix}\]

It’s easy to show this is unitary (i.e. that $P^\dagger = P^{-1}$). With a little more hard labour, leaning on this:

\[e^{i\theta} = \cos \theta + i \sin \theta\]

and being super careful with those minus signs, folks, we can wrap the diagonalised rotation matrix in the usual transform/undo sandwich:

\[P \begin{bmatrix} e^{i\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta} \end{bmatrix} P^\dagger = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta \end{bmatrix}\]

So by twisting these two complex basis vectors, $\ket{v_+}$ anticlockwise and $\ket{v_-}$ clockwise, by some phase angle, we have the effect of an ordinary rotation on our embedded real space. This is how an arbitrary rotation can be diagonalised, something that would be impossible in a real vector space.

And as a result, not just one but two of the most important kinds of operator we need in QM can be understood as diagonal matrices, and thus like operations that act independently on separate coordinate channels.
entry.summary: A digression before we get back to quantum computing. In our previous linear algebra tomfoolery, something important has been bubbling away, which is the importance of diagonal matrix representation, and what they mean for simplicity. They mean that we can think of the dimensions of the space as being like completely separate, isolated channels, which don’t suffer from any “crosstalk”. It’s like you’re doing several completely independent calculations, with no interference between them.

entry.title: Quantumania 15 - Mystery Function
entry.content:
In electronics and regular computing, a gate is a function that takes one or more bit inputs and produces a bit output. Physically bits are represented by voltage levels in wires. A transistor is a switch that can either connect or disconnect two of its terminals so that a current can either flow through them or be blocked: what controls the switch is the voltage level at a third terminal, called the base or gate. A simplistic conceptual use case (not actually how these things are implemented):

  • If you connect two transistors in series, a current can’t flow through them unless they are both switched on (conducting), so in this configuration they implement a gate called AND: Their bases receive the input bits, and if both are $1$, the output is $1$, otherwise the output is $0$.
  • If you connect them in parallel, a current will be able to flow if either of them is on, so they implement an OR gate: if either input is $1$, the output is $1$.

In this way we can make building blocks of complex logic functions. Eventually if you keep playing with this idea, things will get out of hand, which is why your phone has 20 billion transistors in it, and 20 trillion transistors are manufactured every second, and we probably make more of them in a year than the number of individual grains of rice that have ever been eaten by people, and now we can have intelligent conversations with clusters of transistors.

Now, as it happens, transistors absolutely depend on semiconductor behaviour that can’t be explained classically. So in a sense, all computing is quantum computing. But that’s not what we mean by it. We’re actually talking about replacing:

  • the bit as the unit of information, operated on by logic gates and assembled into registers of bits, wherein the states of individual bits remain independent, with
  • the qubit, operated on by unitary transformations (which we’ll still call gates), and assembled into registers of qubits, wherein the individual qubits might not have independent states at all, so the assembly can only be understood as a whole.

That thing where you have only 30 qubits and yet this requires a billion-dimensional state space to give weight to every possible combination of their states, we want to take advantage of that somehow.

Starting off small, the most simple logical functions have a single bit input and a single bit output. In fact there are only four such functions! Two depend on their input, and two ignore it. The first two are the identity function (output is equal to input) and NOT (output is opposite of input). The other two are effectively constants, evaluating always $1$ or always $0$.

Operations on a single qubit are unitary, so they are described by a matrix U that has an inverse (they are always reversible) given by $U^\dagger$, meaning that if you apply the matrix and its conjugate transpose, the state vector is left as it was in the first place, i.e. the combination is equal to the identity matrix:

\[U U^\dagger = I\]

Bonus points if $U = U^\dagger$ (it’s hermitian) too because then it is self-inverse:

\[U U = I\]

So we already have an infinite range of operators we can apply to a single qubit. As with any linear operator, we can fully describe what it does by stating the results of applying it to the basis vectors, and indeed that is what the two columns of the matrix tell us. Take for example the spin matrix for the X axis, expressed in the Z basis (which is shorter than the fancy name: “the computational basis”):

\[X = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

This swaps the coordinates. So it maps:

\[\ket{0} \to \ket{1} \quad \quad \ket{1} \to \ket{0}\]

or in column vector form:

\[(1, 0)^\intercal \to (0, 1)^\intercal \quad \quad (0, 1)^\intercal \to (1, 0)^\intercal\]

This is sometimes called the quantum NOT gate, but it is as likely to be called X in deference to its physical significance. Another one we saw, geometrically just the same thing but acting along a different alignment, is the Hadamard gate:

\[H = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\]

This turns the unit vectors of the computational basis into unit vectors of the X basis (which we’ve often been calling front $\ket{f}$ and back $\ket{b}$):

\[\ket{0} \to \ket{+} \quad \quad \ket{1} \to \ket{-}\]

which are themselves balanced superpositions:

\[\ket{+} = \frac{\ket{0} + \ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \quad \ket{-} = \frac{\ket{0} - \ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\]

And because it’s self-inverse:

\[\ket{+} \to \ket{0} \quad \quad \ket{-} \to \ket{1}\]

Getting more cocky, we can think of gates (unitary transformations) that act on pairs of qubits. One of these is controlled-NOT or CNOT for short. This has a transistor-like quality to it. The state space is 4D, there are 4 basis states, so we have to say what effect the gate has on all four:

\[\ket{00} \to \ket{00} \quad \quad \ket{01} \to \ket{01} \quad \quad \ket{10} \to \ket{11} \quad \quad \ket{11} \to \ket{10}\]

See how it works? The first qubit is the control, so if it’s $0$ then the second qubit is unaffected, but if it’s $1$ the second qubit is flipped. Another way to look at it is that the second qubit is like the output of the classical XOR gate, which can be thought of as a “difference detector”: if the two inputs are the same, the output is $0$, otherwise it’s $1$. But that alone would lose information, something that happens freely in classical computing (one of the reasons why computers need fans - to blow away all the waste entropy1.) By carrying the first qubit through unchanged, it retains the ability to be unitary.

One standard way to write XOR in this context is $\oplus$, meaning “addition, modulo 2”, i.e. divide by $2$ and keep the remainder (or to put it another way, if the result exceeds $1$, subtract $2$ from it until it doesn’t.) With this notation, CNOT is just (with commas for clarity):

\[\ket{A, B} \to \ket{A, A \oplus B}\]

where $A, B \in \lbrace 0, 1 \rbrace$, so this expands to the four possibilities given previously.

Remember, although in this specification $A$ and $B$ can only be the definite symbols $0$ and $1$, giving only the four base state combinations, the operator can apply to any state vector, which can be described by a linear combination of those four ingredients. We’ve already said enough to know what it does, because thanks to linearity, we can just apply the operator to the base ingredients (which we already have prescribed answers for) and make the same linear combination of the results.

Some of the earliest insights into the possibilities of computing this way involved considering a unitary operation formed from an unknown function on classical bits. We realised above that there are only four such functions (identity, NOT and the constants $0$ and $1$). But suppose we have one of them, and we don’t know which one, but someone has conveniently wrapped it in a unitary transform for us, $U_f$:

\[U_f \ket{A, B} = \ket{A, B \oplus f(A)}\]

i.e. the second qubit is XOR between the second qubit’s label and $f$ applied to the first qubit’s label. Again, $A$ and $B$ are only allowed to be $0$ or $1$, and the function $f$ only operates on ordinary bits given by those labels, and yet we’ve fully specified a linear operator that can act on any state, by distributing itself down to each contribution to that state made by a basis state such as $\ket{00}, \ket{01}$… That is, there’s nothing fuzzy happening here. It can all be worked out.

If we have a pair of qubits in the base states $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$, which means as a combined system they are in the base state $\ket{01}$, we can put each of them through Hadamard:

\[\ket{01} \to \ket{+-}\] \[\begin{eqnarray*} \ket{+-} &=& \left[\frac{\ket{0}}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \left[\frac{\ket{0}}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \\ &=& \frac{\ket{00}}{2} - \frac{\ket{01}}{2} + \frac{\ket{10}}{2} - \frac{\ket{11}}{2} \end{eqnarray*}\]

Then we put them through $U_f$. This is a simple enough scenario that we can describe the effect of all flavours of $f$ (and thus $U_f$) on all the base states in full, and so completely grasp what’s going on. What does applying $U_f$ do?

\[U_f \ket{+-} = \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \ket{0, f(0)} - \ket{0, 1 \oplus f(0)} + \ket{1, f(1)} - \ket{1, 1 \oplus f(1)} \Big]\]

But as there are only four possible things $f$ could be, we can write down all four variants of the above gibberish. If $f$ is the identity function, outputting its input unchanged:

\[U_f \ket{+-} = \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \ket{00} - \ket{01} + \ket{11} - \ket{10} \Big]\]

Or if it’s NOT, flipping its input:

\[U_f \ket{+-} = \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \ket{01} - \ket{00} + \ket{10} - \ket{11} \Big]\]

Or if it ignores its input and is always $0$:

\[U_f \ket{+-} = \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \ket{00} - \ket{01} + \ket{10} - \ket{11} \Big]\]

Or is always $1$:

\[U_f \ket{+-} = \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \ket{01} - \ket{00} + \ket{11} - \ket{10} \Big]\]

The difference is in the pattern of positive and negative factors. Tabulating them systematically:

$f$ $\ket{00}$ $\ket{01}$ $\ket{10}$ $\ket{11}$
Identity $+$ $-$ $-$ $+$
NOT $-$ $+$ $+$ $-$
$0$ $+$ $-$ $+$ $-$
$1$ $-$ $+$ $-$ $+$

There are really two patterns here, each containing two variants that only differ by an overall factor of $-1$. If the function pays attention to its input, that is, $f(0) \ne f(1)$:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} U_f \ket{+-} &=& \pm \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \ket{00} - \ket{01} - \ket{10} + \ket{11} \Big] \\ &=& \pm \left[\frac{\ket{0}}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \left[\frac{\ket{0}}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \\ &=& \pm \ket{--} \end{eqnarray*}\]

Whereas if $f$ ignores its input, $f(0) = f(1)$:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} U_f \ket{+-} &=& \pm \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \ket{00} - \ket{01} + \ket{10} - \ket{11} \Big] \\ &=& \pm \left[\frac{\ket{0}}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \left[\frac{\ket{0}}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \\ &=& \pm \ket{+-} \end{eqnarray*}\]

So after this, the first qubit is either $\ket{-}$ or $\ket{+}$, and this tells us if $f$ depends on or ignores its input. Now, we have plenty of measurement devices aligned for the $\lbrace0, 1\rbrace$ basis (a.k.a. the computational basis), and so to save us the trouble of having to buy a detector for the $\lbrace+, -\rbrace$ (X) basis (have you priced those things lately? I’m not made of money!), we can throw the first qubit through a Hadamard gate so it can switch back like this:

\[\ket{+} \to \ket{0} \quad \quad \ket{-} \to \ket{1}\]

And so if we get $0$, we know $f$ is a constant. The first strange thing about this procedure is that we read the useful output from the first qubit, while the second is in an already known, predetermined state and carries no information for us. This is despite the fact that $U_f$ is defined as changing the second qubit, not the first:

\[U_f \ket{A, B} = \ket{A, B \oplus f(A)}\]

But that’s just the definition of it in terms of the computational basis. When we put the qubits through Hadamard we reflected them into the X basis, and the definition doesn’t directly say what it does in that basis in such a simple way, although as we’ve seen, as a linear operator, it does indirectly specify its effect completely regardless of the basis being used.

The other surprising thing is that with a single evaluation of $U_f$, we appear to have narrowed down the identity of $f$ from four possibilities to two. However, this alone seems less impressive when you consider what would happen if you directly evaluated $f$ once. We can classify $f$ variants into subgroups two ways:

  • Is it constant or balanced (dependent on its input)?
  • What’s the output from $f(0)$?

We can arrange the four variants into a matrix according to these criteria:

  constant balanced
$f(0) = 0$ $0$ Identity
$f(0) = 1$ $1$ NOT

So our quantum evaluation technique tells us which column it’s in, whereas classical direct evaluation tells us which row. Both methods halve the possibilities, but… along different axes? How strange.

entry.title: Quantumania 14 - Schrödinger’s Umlaut
entry.content:
Before we get back to that exciting word “gate”, let’s consider some actual physics. Yes, weird, I know. Also I’m going to immediately break the rule-slash-guideline I set for myself last time, where $\hat{H}$ was forever going to stand for Hadamard. Well, this time it’s going to stand for Hamiltonian. This is an operator that characterises the energy of a system, and is something that QM inherits wholesale from classical physics.

Suppose you could measure the energy of a system. For now we’ll gloss over what energy actually is (it’s a deep, circular topic.) Instead, just as we thought of spin orientation along a chosen axis as something we could measure about a system, now we’re saying there’s a numerical quantity called the energy of the system that we can also measure. The state vector encodes everything there is to know about the state of the system, so it has all the information there is about the energy too.

So as always in a two dimensional QM system, anything about it we can measure can only have two possible values. For energy we’ll call them $E_1$ and $E_2$. These are just real numbers. QM tells us to throw these values into a diagonal matrix, $\operatorname{diag}(E_1, E_2)$:

\[\operatorname{diag}(E_1, E_2) = \begin{bmatrix} E_1 & 0 \\ 0 & E_2 \end{bmatrix}\]

There is something particularly important about energy: it is connected with how the state vector of the system changes as time passes. I teased this when complaining about the so-called measurement problem.

QM gives us probability distributions over measurement outcomes that occur when we “make an observation”, a kind of interaction that discontinuously snaps the state vector into alignment with an eigenvector of the observable’s hermitian operator, but the dynamics of the theory contain nothing to suggest this actually ever happens, which is, on the face of it, ridiculous. Now we’re going to examine what the theory does allow to happen to a state vector as time passes.

We’re in effect saying that our state vector is a function of time: $\ket{\psi(t)}$. But one claim we’ve made about QM is that the state vector contains every scintilla of physical information about the system. This means it knows the future! As usual the easiest first step is to align our state vector with a basis vector, that is, an eigenvector of the observable in question. Let’s label the eigenvectors for the two energy levels $\ket{E_1}$ and $\ket{E_2}$. At “the beginning” when $t = 0$:

\[\ket{\psi(0)} = \ket{E_1}\]

In that case, what happens as time passes is:

\[\ket{\psi(t)} = \ket{E_1} e^{-i E_1 t / \hbar}\]

That is, it’s just a pure unit phase factor, and $\hbar$ is defined as $h/2\pi$, where $h$ is Planck’s constant, which is ~$6.6 \times 10^{-34}$. This means the phase factor is oscillating with frequency $\nu = E_1 / h$ (one of the earliest formulae discovered in QM was $E = h \nu$, the Planck relation.) Actual physical implementations of qubits have energies of the order of $10^{-24}$ joules, so the frequency is in the GHz range. This thing is, notionally at least, “spinning” pretty fast.

But because it’s just an overall unit phase factor, this means the alignment of the state vector is not changing. In terms of the physical difference this makes to the state of an isolated system, it’s like multiplying by 1. Physically it means nothing’s happening. The energy, if it was to be measured, would be $E_1$, forever.

But $\ket{\psi(0)}$ doesn’t have to be one of the eigenstates. It could be any unit vector in the state space, which, if we choose to write it in terms of the energy eigenstates, would be some combination of them that comes out as a unit vector.

\[\ket{\psi(0)} = \alpha \ket{E_1} + \beta \ket{E_2}\]

But the complex phase factor spinning as time passes applies to both components:

\[\ket{\psi(t)} = \alpha \ket{E_1} e^{-i E_1 t / \hbar} + \beta \ket{E_2} e^{-i E_2 t / \hbar}\]

Each has its own frequency given by its energy level. $\ket{E_1}$ and $\ket{E_2}$ are the unit vectors of the basis we’re working in:

\[\ket{E_1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad\quad \ket{E_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

So scaling each and summing them is a trivial thing:

\[\ket{\psi(t)} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha e^{-i E_1 t / \hbar} \\ \beta e^{-i E_2 t / \hbar} \end{bmatrix}\]

The spinning phase factors, scaled by the initial coordinates, just become the time-dependent coordinates of the vector in this basis. Although nothing is changing in the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ factors, the relative phase of the two coordinates is going absolutely bonkers.

What does this mean? Refer back to the Bloch sphere, which began as a way to define the state of a qubit in terms of a pair of orthogonal basis states and two real parameters: the inter-coordinate mixing factor, $\theta$, and the phase difference, $\phi$:

\[\ket{\psi} = \cos \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) \ket{u} + e^{i\phi} \sin \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) \ket{d}\]

and ended up with the realisation that it actually directly describes physical directions in space as points on a sphere, given by the angles $(\theta, \phi)$. Changing the relative phase changes the direction in physical space represented by the state vector, moving around the Bloch sphere in a circle of constant latitude.

Can we say the qubit is continuously changing the direction it is pointing in, in physical space? This is considered a step too far. The least controversial thing we can say is that, if you were to choose an alignment in physical space to measure its orientation along, at any given time there is theoretically one specific alignment along which you’d get a definite answer, but you have no idea what that is, because the exact phase difference at any moment is unknown to you, being impossible to discover, and is oscillating rather quickly.

But doesn’t this suggest there something special about the energy eigenvectors and the directions in space they relate to? We’ve always been clear that the observable spin orientation is something that can have any alignment in physical space. Space has rotational symmetry. There are no “special” directions.

Well, if your qubit is the spin state of an electron, that changes the moment you apply a uniform magnetic field across it. The magnetic field has an orientation, and so in effect picks out a special alignment across the electron. If the electron’s spin at the moment you switch the field on happened to be perfectly aligned with the magnetic field, then it will stay aligned with it. The state vector’s corresponding point on the Bloch sphere will stay put. But if it was misaligned, the spin will precess - or I mean to say, the point on the Bloch sphere will trace out a circle, at a fixed latitude, around the pole.

This is why the Hamiltonian, the operator representing the energy observable, is built directly from those same reflection operators we saw last time, most conveniently the diagonal Z matrix form $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$.

I know it’s said that the state vector captures everything there is to know about the system and thus allows us to predict what will happen to it in the future, but this is a somewhat misleading claim. The Hamiltonian isn’t exactly part of the state vector: it’s something else that could vary, and it acts on the state vector to give it a pattern of evolution as time passes. So the whole system, in this model, includes the state vector and the Hamiltonian. The alignment of the Hamiltonian gives us a natural coordinate system within which to define the state vector.

entry.title: Quantumania 13 - The Hadamard Gate
entry.content:
So Hermitian operators represent observables, and their eigenvectors are post-measurement orthogonal vectors, who eigenvalues are the measurement results. That is, if you apply the operator to a unit eigenvector, it will be scaled by an eigenvalue that tells you what the measurement result would be if the state vector was exactly that eigenvector.

When measuring the state of a qubit along Z, the possible results are $+1$ and $-1$, and so we can pack these into a diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$, and that is the Hermitian operator for the observable “measure along Z”, expressed in the Z basis.

But one direction is no different from another: space is symmetrical like that. So there must be similar matrices for the other two spatial directions, but still expressed in the Z basis. If we expressed them in the X basis, then the Hermitian matrix for X would be $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$. Switching the basis to another one of these canonical directions can often just mean switching the labels between the same matrices. Expressed in the Z basis then, they are:

\[Z = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \quad X = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad Y = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

So remember that the X and Y matrices are really the same as Z, but applied inside a “unitary sandwich”, $UZU^\dagger$. So as we can see Z is essentially a reflection, flipping the sign of the $\ket{d}$ coordinate, so must the other two be, just disguised by being expressed in a foreign basis. In geometrical terms, they’re the same operator twisted to act in different directions (technical term: “unitarily equivalent.”)

Now, here the letters used for standard things are unfortunately going to get egregiously confusing, as they so often do. I’ve been using $U$ to stand for any unitary operator, and $H$ for whatever hermitian operator. But there is a super handy unitary operator named after Jacques Hadamard, and tempting as it is to call it $J$, I’m going to have go with normal practice and label it $H$ (and try to avoid using that to stand for any hermitian operator from now on):

\[H = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\]

Fortunately it is hermitian, as well as unitary! These are not mutually exclusive categories. Where both apply:

\[H = H^\dagger = H^{-1}\]

Unitary means that its conjugate transpose is its inverse, and hermitian means it is its own conjugate transpose. So an operator that is both therefore must be its own inverse. Apply it twice and you get back to where you started.

The role it’s playing here is not a QM measurement operator, but a unitary transform corresponding to a $90^\circ$ rotational change of basis in physical space. If we sandwich it around Z matrix, we get the X matrix:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} HZH^\dagger &=& HZH \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{eqnarray*}\]

But as it is its own inverse, if we do the same sandwich trick with the X matrix, we get back to the Z matrix. It flips between the two. We can interpret this as either a transformation we can apply to a state vector, or a change of basis that takes us between the Z and X bases. It’s yet another a chance to admire our favourite diagram:

Sometimes it’s said that $H$ works like a combination of a $45^\circ$ anticlockwise rotation, followed by a reflection around the axis that the $\ket{f}$ vector lies on. To see how this explanation works, first start with $\ket{u}$:

  • rotate it $45^\circ$ anticlockwise, now it’s $\ket{f}$,
  • reflect it around $\ket{f}$, that has no effect on it, so the final result is $\ket{f}$.

Then start with $\ket{d}$:

  • rotate it $45^\circ$ anticlockwise, now it’s pointing the opposite direction to $\ket{b}$,
  • reflect it around $\ket{f}$, that flips it around to $\ket{b}$.

So $\ket{u}$ becomes $\ket{f}$, while $\ket{d}$ becomes $\ket{b}$. Then try going the other way - start from $\ket{f}$:

  • rotation takes us to $\ket{d}$,
  • reflection goes back to $\ket{u}$.

And finally from $\ket{b}$:

  • rotation takes to $\ket{u}$,
  • reflection to $\ket{d}$.

How does it achieve these miracles? What, fundamentally, is it, in geometrical terms? For the three observable direction matrices X, Y and Z, we know they are fundamentally all the same thing: a simple reflection. The only difference is that they’ve been sandwiched between some unitary rotation “bread”… wait a second!

Could it be that $H$ is also unitarily equivalent to $Z$? Yes it could. All four of these matrices are geometrically the same thing: a reflection, just aligned along different axes.

Look how ridiculously simple it actually is: just pure reflection around that dotted line on the $\pi/8$ axis, bisecting the angle between $\ket{u}$ and $\ket{f}$.

There are good reasons for sometimes thinking of it as a rotation by $\pi/4$ followed by a reflection around the $\pi/4$ axis, one of which is that the implementation of this operation in a quantum computer may be composed of successive operations in exactly that way.
entry.summary: So Hermitian operators represent observables, and their eigenvectors are post-measurement orthogonal vectors, who eigenvalues are the measurement results. That is, if you apply the operator to a unit eigenvector, it will be scaled by an eigenvalue that tells you what the measurement result would be if the state vector was exactly that eigenvector.

entry.title: Quantumania 12 - Unexpected Values
entry.content:
We’ve encountered two kinds of operator, unitary (including rotations, reflections and phase factors), and hermitian (the kind that scales in orthogonal directions.)

In QM the role of hermitian operators is to represent observables. This sounds more abstract than it actually is: we’ve seen how if you have a qubit, its state vector can be pointing in any direction in the state space (which corresponds to a direction in physical space), but to find anything out about it you have to choose an alignment in physical space, and the only thing you can discover is a single bit (in information theory terms): which way along your chosen alignment it points (as of now, since you measured it.) Each possible answer corresponds to a different post-measurement state vector, and for one observable, all the possible post-measurement state vectors are mutually orthogonal.

Every observable has a hermitian operator that scales along its post-measurement alignments. So the $\ket{u}$ and $\ket{d}$ vectors of the Z basis get scaled differently by the operator for “measure along Z”. If we represent the operator as a matrix in the Z basis, it’s a diagonal matrix, and the values on the diagonal are the eigenvalues. For $\ket{u}$, the value is $+1$ and for $\ket{d}$, it’s $-1$.

Now, we know that the state vector’s coordinates in a measurement basis are each directly related to the probability of getting the measurement outcome represented by that coordinate’s basis vector. The modulus squared of the coordinate is the probability, which we get by multiplying the coordinate by its complex conjugate.

And we just learned that we can do this for all the coordinates, sum them, and get $1$, expressed by this notation, a bra-ket combination:

\[\braket{\psi}{\psi}\]

which in terms of matrices is just matrix multiplication between the column vector on the right and a row vector on the left, the latter containing the complex conjugates of the coordinates on the right. This literally just means we’re finding the modulus squared of all the coordinates and summing them. An exhaustive set of mutually exclusive probabilities has to sum to $1$, but also this is the inner product of a unit vector with itself, which also means it has the value $1$.

So what happens if we insert our hermitian operator for our observable in the middle?

\[\bra{\psi} H \ket{\psi}\]

The symmetry of the notation is indicative of the associative nature of matrix multiplication: it doesn’t matter which side we multiply first. But the extra ingredient provided by the central operator is the measured values: the eigenvalues associated with each measurement outcome. Because it’s a diagonal matrix (in its own basis), there’s no “crosstalk” between the dimensions. Each coordinate is being scaled by its measurable value, as well as being converted into a probability, so we’re in effect multiplying measurable values by the probability of obtaining them, and finally summing all those numbers.

This is the probability-weighted average of the measurable values, often called the expectation value by physicists, and unfortunately called the “expected” value in many other fields. Why unfortunate? Because it may well be a value that it is impossible to measure in any given experiment, so it hardly seems right to call it expected. Then again, “expectation” isn’t super clear about that either. It’s really the average result of making the same measurement many times on identically prepared systems.

The notation for it is also a bit confusing in this context:

\[\langle H \rangle\]

It looks like we’ve erased the state vectors from Dirac’s notation, but this is just a notational overlap. The angle brackets are used for the expectation value of a variable in statistics, never mind QM.

Here’s how it works when our observable is “measure along the Z axis”, so our basis vectors are $\ket{u}$ and $\ket{d}$ and their eigenvalues are $+1$ and $-1$ respectively, meaning that $Z = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$. We’re going to work out:

\[\langle Z \rangle = \bra{\psi} Z \ket{\psi}\]

Expressing our state vector as a linear combination of the basis vectors (I’ve once again chosen numbers that will come out neat when squared):

\[\ket{\psi} = 0.8367 \ket{u} + 0.5477 \ket{d}\]

Apply $Z$ to it (it just flips the sign of the down coordinate):

\[Z \ket{\psi} = 0.8367 \ket{u} - 0.5477 \ket{d}\]

And finally applying $\bra{\psi}$:

\[\langle Z \rangle = 0.7 - 0.3 = 0.4\]

The only values we can possibly measure are $+1$ and $-1$, but the expectation value comes out as $0.4$, because I set up $\ket{\psi}$ to be weighted more toward up than down. If I’d made both coordinates $1/\sqrt{2}$ then $\langle Z \rangle$ would have come out as zero, and if $\ket{\psi} = \ket{u}$ then it would simply be $1$.

entry.title: Quantumania 11 - Daggers, Bras and Kets
entry.content:
By this point you could be forgiven for wondering what any of this has to do with QM. Let’s bring in complex numbers. If our vector space has complex scalars, then our matrices that operate on it can have complex entries. In terms of direct visualisation of the impact of such a matrix, good luck with that, but broadly speaking, it should be clear that we can still write a diagonal matrix and that it will scale along the coordinate axes. Likewise we can apply rotations:

\[U = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b^* \\ b & a^* \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{where } \vert a \vert^2 + \vert b \vert^2 = 1\]

Note that this time I haven’t jumped straight to writing it with entries $\cos \theta$ etc. I’ve just given the constraint about the squared-moduli of $a$ and $b$ summing to $1$.

This has to do with one of the defining characteristics of a rotation, which is that the vectors all stay the same length.

Pythagoras computes the length of a vector from its coordinates. It looks like $a$ and $b$ are acting like vector coordinates in that constraint, except they’re complex, so we’re taking the modulus squared.

There’s a way to get the modulus squared of a complex number, $z$, which is to multiply it by its complex conjugate, $z^*$, which we get by flipping the sign of the imaginary part:

\[z = p + qi\] \[z^* = p - qi\] \[z z^* = (p + qi)(p - qi) = p^2 - pqi + pqi - q^2i^2 = p^2 + q^2\]

Look how they Pythagorised my boy! There is nothing surprising about this: flipping the sign of $qi$ is like reflecting in the real axis, so if you think of a complex number as a rotation factor, its conjugate rotates the other way. So conjugation on the polar form is like this:

\[z = r e^{i\theta}\] \[z^* = \left(r e^{i\theta}\right)^* = r e^{-i\theta}\]

So multiplying a complex number by its own conjugate rotates it back to the real number line, cancelling out the rotation, and guaranteeing the result is a real number, the square of the modulus:

\[z z^* = r e^{i\theta} \left(r e^{i\theta}\right)^* = r^2 e^{i\theta} e^{-i\theta} = r^2\]

So this is how we get a real, non-negative “length” of an individual complex number. But in our complex vector spaces, we’d like the length of a vector to also be real and non-negative. Let’s write Pythagoras for the whole vector $\vec{v}$ with two complex coordinates $(v_1, v_2)$:

\[\Vert \vec{v} \Vert^2 = v_1 v_1^* + v_2 v_2^*\]

Now, there’s a massively important thing about our vector spaces we’ve got this far without mentioning, but here it comes: the inner product. This is a general term for the same thing as the dot product we use with regular vectors.

This is a function that takes two vectors and outputs a scalar, and it is the essential link between a dry column-vector space like $R^2$ and the world of geometry. The inner product of two orthogonal vectors is $0$. And crucially the inner product of a vector with itself is the squared length of the vector. Now, looking at the above formula for the length of the vector, it strongly suggests that the inner product of two vectors $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{w}$ should be:

\[(\vec{v}, \vec{w}) = v_1 w_1^* + v_2 w_2^*\]

simply because if we substitute $\vec{v}$ in place of $\vec{w}$ then we’ll get back our length-squared formula, as we must. This is the same thing as taking the complex conjugate of all the coordinates of one vector, before applying the usual dot product formula we’re familiar with from real vector spaces.

Also we can rewrite the dot product as matrix multiplication if we transpose the left vector from a column to a row. So that we put all this fiddling around onto one of the vectors instead of sharing it out, let’s define the superscripted symbol $\dagger$ to mean:

  • transpose the matrix, and
  • take the complex conjugate of all its entries.

So we can just define the inner product of the column vectors $v$ and $w$ as $v^\dagger$ $w$. The left column vector $v$ is transposed into a row, all its entries are conjugated, and then ordinary matrix multiplication with $w$ does the rest.

I’ve mostly been writing vectors in the strange QM way: $\ket{\psi}$. This is really one half of the notation invented by Dirac. The other half is:

\[\bra{\psi} \equiv \psi^\dagger\]

In other words, $\ket{\psi}$ is an abstract vector plucked from the space. Then $\psi$ is a concrete representation of it in a particular basis as a column of numbers. By applying the $^\dagger$ operator to it, we turn it into a row containing the complex-conjugated coordinates of $\psi$. And we can take this as being the concrete representation of a fundamentally different object, $\bra{\psi} $, albeit one that is paired uniquely with $ \ket{\psi}$.

What is the nature of this new object? It is in fact (unsurprisingly, given its concrete representation) another kind of vector, from a different vector space, but it can be thought of a function that acts on the original, ordinary type of vector. The terminology in this area is so varied you can take your pick of names, but in physics they call $\bra{\psi} $ a bra and $ \ket{\psi}$ a ket. When a bra (function) acts on a ket (input), we have a bra-ket (Dirac thought this was funny):

\[\braket{\psi}{\psi}\]

In that example, as both sides say $\psi$, and assuming that’s a state vector, the answer should be 1, because the result is the squared length, and it better be a unit vector.

It has a double meaning: in abstract, it’s a sort of geometrical function acting on a vector, a geometrical object, to produce a scalar. In concrete terms, when we’ve expressed both sides in compatible bases as row and column vectors, it’s matrix multiplication.

So when we talk about the inner product between two vectors in QM, what we really mean is that we have two kets, and we’re going to convert one of them into a bra in the standard way, and let that bra act on the ket. This is most often assumed without stating it explicitly, so you might say you’re going to take the inner product of $\ket{a}$ and $\ket{b}$ and so that’s $\braket{a}{b}$. It’s a given that you’re going to have switch one of them to a bra.

Does it matter which? Yes: these are mutual complex conjugates:

\[\braket{b}{a} = \braket{a}{b}^*\]

Whenever you see that bra-ket shape, you’re looking at a scalar. The most helpful way to think about the purpose of a bra is to think of a basis vector, such as $\ket{u}$, and suppose that you have a state vector $\ket{\psi}$ and you want to know its coordinate in the direction of $\ket{u}$. It’s just:

\[\braket{u}{\psi}\]

So I can make a column vector of the coordinates in the up/down basis:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \braket{u}{\psi} \\ \braket{d}{\psi} \\ \end{bmatrix}\]

And I can (somewhat unnecessarily) reconstruct the whole vector by scaling the basis vectors by the coordinates in that basis:

\[\ket{\psi} = \braket{u}{\psi} \ket{u} + \braket{d}{\psi} \ket{d}\]

I’m scaling the two basis vectors by the coordinates, but I’ve got those coordinates by fetching them out of $\ket{\psi}$. Of course, if $\ket{\psi}$ is already known to me as a column vector in that basis, then fetching a coordinate from it isn’t that arduous. It’s right there, in the column vector! But the neat thing about this geometrically is that we can work in any basis. If I have $\ket{\psi}$ and the up/down basis vectors as column vectors all expressed in the front/back basis, the above expressions all produce the same results.

Let’s return to our general rotation matrix and look at how it works. It’s all the way up the page by now so here it is again:

\[U = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b^* \\ b & a^* \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{where } \vert a \vert^2 + \vert b \vert^2 = 1\]

You may recall that we can understand what a matrix does to the unit vectors of its basis by simply reading the columns. The first column is the result it produces when it acts on $(1, 0)^\intercal$, the second column is the same for $(0, 1)^\intercal$.

I mentioned earlier that one of the defining characteristics of a rotation is that the vectors all stay the same length. What I didn’t mention is that it must also preserve the angle between pairs of vectors. Now, by definition our unit vectors are orthogonal before we rotate them:

\[\braket{u}{d} = 0\]

After we rotate them they should be the same length and still be orthogonal.

Reading the columns of the matrix, after we rotate them the vectors have coordinates $(a, b)$ and $(-b^\ast, a^\ast)$. So the inner product is:

\[-ab + ba = 0\]

They’re still orthogonal, mission accomplished. But are they both still unit vectors? Easy enough to find out, because we just take the inner product of each with itself:

\[a^2 + b^2 \quad \text{and} \quad b b^* + a a^*\]

The only way to ensure those both come out as 1 is to require that:

\[\vert a \vert^2 + \vert b \vert^2 = 1\]

I mentioned yesterday that for a rotation (or reflection) matrix in a real vector space we can get its inverse by simply transposing it. In a complex vector space we have to upgrade this to using the full $^{\dagger}$ approach:

\[U^\dagger = U^{-1}\]

It’s easy to check that this works, because if you multiply a matrix by its inverse, that should give you $I$, the identity matrix, and so:

\[UU^\dagger = I\]

So we just need to multiply our general $U$ by $U^\dagger$ and see what we get:

\[UU^{\dagger} = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b^* \\ b & a^* \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a^* & b^* \\ -b & a \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} aa^* + bb^* & ab^* - ab^* \\ ba^* - ba^* & bb^* + aa^* \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}\]

In the last step, we’re using the fact that our general rotation matrix stipulates that $\vert a \vert^2 + \vert b \vert^2 = 1$, and the previously noted rule that $aa^* = \vert a \vert$.

As well as rotating Stick Man, we also applied a kind of orthogonal scaling operation to him, which:

  • is represented by a symmetric matrix (equal to its own transpose),
  • picks out a set of orthogonal directions in the vector space along which it scales, suitable for basis vectors to point along (its eigenbasis) and
  • can always be represented by a diagonal matrix, simply by writing its own eigenbasis.

There’s one aspect of this we need to upgrade for complex vector spaces. We have a reason in QM for wanting the scaling factors to be restricted to real numbers, so when stated in its simple diagonal form, the entries $x$, $y$ on the diagonal are real numbers:

\[H = \begin{bmatrix} x & 0 \\ 0 & y \\ \end{bmatrix}\]

As we noted when stretching/squishing Stick Man, by putting the diagonal form inside a rotation sandwich, we get a matrix that scales along any set of orthogonal directions we like:

\[\begin{bmatrix} a & -b^* \\ b & a^* \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x & 0 \\ 0 & y \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a^* & b^* \\ -b & a \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b^* \\ b & a^* \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} xa^* & xb^* \\ -yb & ya \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} xaa^* + ybb^* & xab^* - yab^* \\ xa^*b - ya^*b & xbb^* + yaa^* \\ \end{bmatrix}\]

Now because $x$ and $y$ are real, and $aa^*$ is the modulus of $a$ and therefore real, the main diagonal entries are real numbers.

Also because real numbers have no imaginary part to negate, they are their own complex conjugates, which means that the off-diagonal entries are mutually complex conjugates:

\[xab^* - yab^* = (xa^*b - ya^*b)^*\]

What that means is that the general form of an orthogonal scaling matrix is not that it is equal to its own transpose, but that it is equal to its conjugate transpose:

\[H = H^{\dagger}\]

That’s the only difference from before. (In fact this is true of the real case too, because the conjugate transpose is equal to the transpose if all the entries in the matrix are real.)

Some updated terminology:

  • The conjugate transpose, indicated by $^{\dagger}$, is often called the hermitian conjugate.
  • A matrix that is equal to its hermitian conjugate is called a hermitian matrix, and represents a hermitian operator (which is why I used $H$ for it in the example above.)
  • A rotation or reflection matrix such as $U$ is called a unitary matrix (which is why I labelled it $U$ above), representing a unitary operator, which preserves the inner product between any pairs of vectors it is applied to.

So now we’ve identified a couple of types of operator and their matrix representations, and it’s high time we found out what they have to do with QM.
